title: Man-Made Fibre Spinning: Melt, Dry and Wet Routes
subtitle: Learn how polymers become filaments, and why the spinning route shapes speed, cost and fibre properties.
card_description: A free reading course on how man-made fibres are made: melt, dry and wet spinning, dry-jet wet and gel spinning, and how each route shapes the fibre.
seo_description: Free course on man-made fibre spinning: how melt, dry and wet spinning work, and how each route affects speed, cost and fibre properties.

source.title: Melt Spinning and Solution Spinning of Man-Made Fibres

outcomes: Explain how man-made fibres are extruded through a spinneret and solidified
Describe the melt spinning sequence, from drying chips to drawing filaments
Explain how drawing and take-up speed affect orientation, tenacity and elongation
Compare dry, wet, dry-jet wet and gel spinning and their typical fibres
Choose a spinning route from polymer behaviour and explain its effect on properties
audience: Textile and fashion students, fibre and yarn buyers, and production or quality staff who want to understand how synthetic and regenerated fibres are made.
about: Polyester, nylon, viscose, acrylic and elastane all start as polymers that must be turned into fine filaments. This free reading course, based on a Fibre2Fashion article by Dr Lipsa Mohapatra, explains how that happens. You will follow melt spinning step by step, from drying polymer chips to quenching and drawing, and see how take-up speed gives LOY, POY and FDY. You will then learn how solution spinning handles polymers that cannot be melted, through dry, wet, dry-jet wet and gel spinning. Finally, you will compare the routes on speed, cost and solvent use, and see how each shapes the finished fibre. A short quiz checks your understanding.

lessons.title: From Polymer to Filament: Melt Spinning
Solution Spinning: Dry and Wet Routes

quiz.q: What mainly decides whether a polymer is melt spun or solution spun?
options: Whether it can be melted without decomposing
The number of holes in the spinneret
The filament cross-section required
Whether the fibre will be cut into staple
quiz.feedback: The route depends mainly on the polymer's thermal behaviour. Polymers that melt without decomposing are melt spun; others must be dissolved and solution spun.

quiz.q: A polyester filament is to have a trilobal cross-section. In melt spinning, what mainly sets this shape?
options: The speed of the take-up rollers
The amount of spin finish applied
The shape of the spinneret holes
The drawing ratio after spinning
quiz.feedback: In melt spinning the spinneret hole is the main control over cross-section, so trilobal holes give trilobal filaments.

quiz.q: What happens to filament properties when as-spun filaments are drawn?
options: Tenacity falls and elongation rises
Tenacity rises and elongation falls
Any remaining solvent is removed
The number of filaments increases
quiz.feedback: Drawing aligns the molecules along the fibre axis, which increases tenacity and reduces elongation.

quiz.q: Which melt-spun yarn form is commonly used as feed yarn for draw-texturing?
options: Fully drawn yarn (FDY)
Low-oriented yarn (LOY)
Wet-spun staple fibre
Partially oriented yarn (POY)
quiz.feedback: POY is spun at higher speeds and is commonly used as draw-texturing feed yarn. LOY needs full drawing, and FDY is already fully drawn.

quiz.q: How does the filament solidify in dry spinning?
options: By coagulation in an acid bath
By cooling in a quench chamber
By cooling a dilute solution into a gel
By solvent evaporating in hot air or inert gas
quiz.feedback: In dry spinning the dope contains a volatile solvent, which evaporates in a heated chamber. The solvent vapour is recovered for reuse.

quiz.q: Why can a dry-spun acrylic filament end up with a dog-bone cross-section?
options: Solidification starts at the filament surface
Quench air flattens the hot filament
The acid bath dissolves its edges
It is cut into staple after spinning
quiz.feedback: In dry spinning, solidification begins at the surface. As solvent then leaves the inside, the filament shrinks and its outline becomes non-circular.

quiz.q: In viscose production, what happens when the dope is extruded into the acid bath?
options: The solvent evaporates into hot air
The polymer melts and then cools
Cellulose is regenerated in filament form
Spin finish is applied to the filaments
quiz.feedback: The xanthate dope is extruded into an acid bath, usually containing sulphuric acid, sodium sulphate and zinc sulphate, where cellulose is regenerated.

quiz.q: What does the air gap in dry-jet wet spinning make possible?
options: Spinning without any solvent
Higher drawing and better molecular orientation
Faster solvent evaporation than dry spinning
Lower polymer molecular weight
quiz.feedback: The filament passes through a small air gap before the bath, which permits higher drawing and improved molecular orientation, as in para-aramid and lyocell.

quiz.q: Wet spinning is the fastest of the three principal spinning methods.
quiz.feedback: Wet spinning is the slowest, because coagulation depends on chemical and diffusion processes. Melt spinning is the fastest.

quiz.q: Which of these fibres are made by solution spinning? (select all that apply)
options: Viscose
Elastane
Polypropylene
Lyocell
Nylon 6,6
quiz.feedback: Viscose (wet), elastane (dry) and lyocell (dry-jet wet) are solution spun. Polypropylene and nylon 6,6 melt without decomposing, so they are melt spun.

glossary.def: A plate with many fine holes through which liquid polymer is extruded to form filaments.
The polymer is melted, extruded and solidified by cooling. Used for polyester, nylon and polypropylene.
The viscous spinning solution made by dissolving a polymer in a solvent for solution spinning.
Solution spinning in which a volatile solvent evaporates in hot air or inert gas, solidifying the filament.
Solution spinning in which filaments solidify in a coagulation bath by solvent exchange or chemical reaction.
Cooling and solidifying melt-spun filaments with a controlled air flow in a quench chamber.
Stretching as-spun filaments to align their molecules, which increases tenacity and reduces elongation.
Low-oriented, partially oriented and fully drawn yarn: melt-spun forms that differ in take-up speed and drawing.
Extrusion through a small air gap into a coagulation bath, allowing higher drawing. Used for para-aramid and lyocell.
A dilute UHMWPE solution is extruded, cooled to a gel filament and drawn to very high ratios.
